title: Savings account or index fund? Use both, for different jobs
summary: Money you might need soon belongs somewhere safe and instant. Money you won't touch for years can be invested. Your 401(k) match comes first.

sections.heading: Money for the next few years: savings
sections.body: A high-yield savings account pays about 3.6% a year, you can take money out instantly, and it is FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor at insured banks. With inflation around 3.4%, that roughly keeps pace with prices. A checking account pays little or nothing, so keep only spending money there.

sections.heading: Money for the long run: index funds
sections.body: A broad stock index fund owns small pieces of hundreds of companies. Its value goes up and down, sometimes a lot, but the long-term average has historically been positive, about 8% a year in our figures. Only invest money you won't need for many years.

sections.heading: Don't skip the 401(k) match
sections.body: A 401(k) is paid in from your paycheck before tax, and many employers add a match. Not taking the match leaves part of your pay on the table. Withdrawing before age 59½ usually costs a 10% penalty plus tax, so treat it as retirement money. Individual IRAs are another option on top of Social Security.

example.title: Maya's three pots
example.body: Maya takes home $3,200 a month and has about $450 left after essentials. She first builds a cushion of three months' expenses in a high-yield savings account. At work, she raises her 401(k) contribution just enough to get her employer's full match. Once the cushion is full, she sends $150 a month into a broad index fund and doesn't check it every day.

takeaway: Cushion first, match second, invest the rest for the long run: each pot has its own job.

quiz.question: Where should the money for next month's rent live?
quiz.why: You need it soon and it must not drop in value. Savings are instant and FDIC-insured; index funds go up and down.

quiz.question: Your employer matches 401(k) contributions. What happens if you don't contribute?
options: You leave part of your pay on the table
quiz.why: The match is extra pay you only get by contributing yourself.

quiz.question: A broad index fund fell 15% this year. What does that tell you about long-term money?
options: Ups and downs are normal; it suits money you won't need for years
quiz.why: Its value swings, but the long-term average has historically been positive, which is why it's for long-term goals.
